title: CVE-2026-94265: Authorization: Negotiate sent to foreign origin
excerpt:
Hi all,

I've discovered that curl can be made to send an "Authorization: Negotiate" header, carrying a freshly minted Kerberos ticket for the victim's ambient identity, to a host chosen by an HTTP redirect, without --location-trusted. All the attacker has to do is put arbitrary userinfo in the Location header they redirect to. This contradicts the guarantee documented for CURLOPT_UNRESTRICTED_AUTH, which says that with the option unset libcurl "does not send custom nor internally generated Authorization: or Cookie: headers on requests done to other hosts than the one used for the initial URL".

I have an end-to-end PoC against a real KDC on pristine upstream d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7 (8.23.0-DEV), a control showing the protection holds when the userinfo is removed, and a small fix that I have verified closes it without regressing either normal Negotiate or --location-trusted. Details below.

How it works
------------

The gate asks "do I have any credentials?" when it should ask "am I still on the original host?"

```
  https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L872-L878

    /* Either we have credentials for the origin we talk to or
       performing authentication is allowed here */
    if(data->state.creds || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))
      result = output_auth_headers(data, conn, authhost, request,
                                   path_and_query, FALSE);
    else
      authhost->done = TRUE;
```

That "||" is the whole vulnerability. Either condition is enough.

The flow:

  1. You run `curl --negotiate -L http://intranet/` - Kerberos SSO, no password typed.
  2. `intranet` redirects you to `http://bob:alice@attacker.example/`.
  3. curl correctly drops *your* credentials, because it is a different host. But it then parses `bob:alice` out of the attacker's own URL and stores it in state.creds. That path has no origin check.
  4. Gate: credentials exist -> proceed. The origin check is never consulted.
  5. The Negotiate branch runs. It throws `bob:alice` away, goes to the KDC, and gets a fresh Kerberos ticket for HTTP/attacker.example. Sends it.

The attacker now holds a Kerberos AP-REQ for their own service, proving your identity.

What makes it odd is that a credential which is never used unlocks an authentication that does not use credentials. `bob:alice` is neither forwarded nor chec

summary: curl sends an Authorization: Negotiate header with a fresh Kerberos ticket to a host chosen by an HTTP redirect without --location-trusted, bypassing the guarantee that such headers are not sent to other hosts.

claims.text: The gate condition `if(data->state.creds || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))` allows authentication to proceed if any credentials are present, without checking that the target host is the original origin.
claims.reasoning: The code at lib/http.c:874 shows the exact condition described. If data->state.creds is truthy (non-NULL), the second operand Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data) is short-circuited and never evaluated, so the origin check is bypassed.

citations.note: Gate condition `if(data->state.creds || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))` allows auth to proceed if state.creds is non-NULL, without requiring the origin check to pass.

claims.text: lib/http.c line 872-878 (gate condition) and lib/url.c lines 1355-1360 (origin-checked credentials) and 1383-1391 (URL‑extracted credentials).
claims.reasoning: The two code paths are present exactly as described: application credentials require Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin, while URL-extracted credentials do not.

citations.note: Application-set credentials are guarded by `Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(data, data->state.origin)` at lines 1355-1360.
URL-extracted credentials (lines 1383-1391) have no origin check; they are parsed from the redirect target URL and stored into state.creds unconditionally.

claims.text: A Location header containing userinfo (e.g., "bob:alice@attacker.example/") causes curl to populate state.creds for the foreign origin, satisfying the gate condition.
claims.reasoning: The URL parsing code at lib/url.c:1383-1391 runs after a redirect and stores attacker-supplied userinfo into state.creds without any origin validation, making the gate at lib/http.c:874 true.

citations.note: When a redirect Location header contains userinfo (e.g., bob:alice@attacker.example), curl_url_get extracts it and the merge at line 1411 populates data->state.creds for the foreign origin.

claims.text: The attacker receives an Authorization: Negotiate header carrying a freshly minted Kerberos ticket for their service, enabling impersonation.
claims.reasoning: The Negotiate branch lacks the cross-host guard that HTTPSIG has. Once the gate passes, output_auth_headers calls Curl_output_negotiate, which builds the SPN from the current (attacker) origin and obtains a fresh Kerberos ticket for it.

citations.note: Negotiate branch (lines 688-701) only checks for absence of a custom Authorization header; it does NOT check Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data), unlike the HTTPSIG branch above (lines 671-684).
Curl_output_negotiate uses data->state.origin->hostname (the attacker's host) to build the SPN, so a fresh ticket is minted for the attacker's service.

claims.text: Run curl with --negotiate --location against a host that redirects to an attacker‑controlled URL containing userinfo; the attacker’s server logs the Authorization header.
claims.reasoning: The reproduction script is detailed and uses only documented curl options (--negotiate, --location, --resolve) without --location-trusted. The deterministic checks confirm the grounded symbols and files exist at the reported revision.

citations.note: The provided script sets up a real Kerberos realm, a legitimate origin that redirects to an attacker origin with userinfo, and demonstrates the Authorization: Negotiate header is sent only in the exploit arm.

key_reasons: The gate at lib/http.c:874 uses `data->state.creds || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data)`, so any non-NULL credentials (including attacker-supplied userinfo from a redirect URL) bypass the origin check.
URL-extracted credentials are stored into state.creds without an origin check (lib/url.c:1383-1391), while application-set credentials are correctly guarded (lib/url.c:1355-1360).
The Negotiate branch in output_auth_headers (lib/http.c:688-701) lacks the Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data) guard that the HTTPSIG branch has (lib/http.c:671-684).
Curl_output_negotiate builds the SPN from data->state.origin->hostname (the attacker's host), causing a fresh Kerberos ticket to be minted for the attacker's service.
The reporter's PoC demonstrates the flaw end-to-end against a real KDC, and the control (no userinfo in redirect) shows the protection works when the trigger is absent.
The suggested fix adds the missing Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data) check to the Negotiate branch, mirroring the HTTPSIG branch.
reply: Thank you for the thorough report and reproduction. The code confirms the flaw: the gate at lib/http.c:874 short-circuits on any credentials, URL-extracted credentials lack an origin check (lib/url.c:1383-1391), and the Negotiate branch omits the cross-host guard that HTTPSIG has (lib/http.c:688-701 vs 671-684). Your fix adding Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data) to the Negotiate condition is correct and mirrors the existing HTTPSIG pattern. We will apply this fix and credit you.
